Comparing data publishing workflows for qualitative research: GitHub to Zenodo and SWISSUbase

Source: vignettes/articles/publishing-workflow.Rmd
publishing-workflow.Rmd

This article is the workflow comparison of the FAIRqual project (work package 1, activity 1.1). It documents how the data in this package were published and compares that route with SWISSUbase, which offers restricted access. The dataitd24 package is the worked example of the GitHub to Zenodo workflow. The SWISSUbase side is based on a walk-through of a deposit in the platform in September 2026.

Introduction

The FAIRqual project aims to enhance the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) of qualitative research data. This report documents and compares two workflows for publishing qualitative research data: the GitHub to Zenodo workflow used at Global Health Engineering (GHE), and the SWISSUbase workflow, which offers more options for restricted data sharing.

The comparison comes from our workshop at the International Transdisciplinarity Conference (ITD24) in Utrecht, where participants consented to share the workshop data openly. This allowed us to consider both workflows for the same dataset.

Background

The need for qualitative data sharing

Sharing qualitative data remains uncommon compared to quantitative data sharing, despite its potential to contribute to sustainability science and broader research synthesis (Alexander et al. 2020). Qualitative data presents its own challenges, including ethical concerns, the need for careful de-identification, and questions about the validity of secondary analysis (Lamb et al. 2024; Campbell et al. 2023).

Two approaches to data publishing

  1. GitHub to Zenodo: an open by default approach that uses version control and automated DOI generation.
  2. SWISSUbase: a national platform, run by FORS with the universities of Neuchâtel and Zurich, with access controls suitable for sensitive or restricted data.

Framework for comparison

Following Alexander et al. (2020), we use their framework of access and processing levels for qualitative data to guide the comparison. It helps researchers decide on a sharing level based on data sensitivity and participant consent.

Workflow comparison

Comparison of the GitHub to Zenodo and SWISSUbase workflows
Step GitHub to Zenodo SWISSUbase
Login registration of an account with an email address national: SWITCH edu-ID; international: CLARIN
Technical knowledge Git basics and the R package tooling web forms only, no Git needed
Data restriction options public or private repository; a private repository gives access to added collaborators, but the data still sits on GitHub servers set per dataset, not per file: open access, or restricted through a deposit contract (named data user, purpose, a term of one to five years, renewable on request)
Structure one dataset per repository, all files in one folder project, then datasets, then files; data files and documentation files are separate types
Metadata machine readable files in the repository (CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json), reused by Zenodo typed by hand into web forms at project and dataset level, no machine readable import; an abstract in English is required
Documentation in the same folder, with dedicated file types for different aspects separate documentation files, which can be public in the catalogue while the data stays restricted
Licence chosen by the depositor, for example CC BY 4.0 set per dataset; the default is non-commercial and can be changed, or reuse is set through a download contract
Version control Git history of every change version history, which does not show who made an edit
File upload as a folder single files or a compressed zip folder
Standard formats open formats above everything CLARIN-CH standard data formats

Authentication and access

GitHub to Zenodo: requires email-based registration. This makes it accessible globally, but can raise concerns about data governance in some jurisdictions.

SWISSUbase: offers two authentication options, national access via SWITCH edu-ID for Swiss institutions and international access through CLARIN for broader academic collaboration. Identity checks come before access to restricted data.

Technical requirements

The GitHub workflow requires familiarity with Git version control, which can be a barrier for researchers without a technical background. SWISSUbase works through web forms with validation messages, for example when the collection mode or the documentation is incomplete. Everything is entered by hand, so the metadata cannot be generated from files in a repository.

Data restriction options

This is the key difference between the platforms. GitHub works on an open by default principle with limited options for controlled access. Private repositories are possible, but they do not meet institutional requirements for sensitive data protection. SWISSUbase sets access per dataset: a dataset is either open or restricted through a deposit contract, so open and restricted material from one study goes into separate datasets of the same project (Enriquez 2024). Documentation, such as interview guides and consent forms, can be public while the data it describes stays restricted.

Version control and long-term preservation

Git version control on GitHub tracks every change and who made it, which supports transparency and reproducibility. SWISSUbase keeps a version history, but it does not show who made an edit. On the GitHub route, long-term preservation comes from the Zenodo archive of each release.

Benefits and limitations

GitHub to Zenodo

Benefits:

  • uses existing developer infrastructure and practices
  • allows rich metadata through several standards (CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json, RO-Crate)
  • supports data curation and documentation through tools like pkgdown
  • DOI generation and versioning through the Zenodo integration
  • platform independent, so the data can move between Git hosting services

Limitations:

  • limited options for controlled or restricted sharing
  • requires technical knowledge that may exclude some researchers
  • data protection concerns due to storage on commercial servers
  • suitable mainly for open by default scenarios

SWISSUbase

Benefits:

  • access controls per dataset, with deposit contracts for restricted data
  • public documentation next to restricted data
  • web forms that require little technical knowledge
  • integration with academic authentication systems
  • structured, project-based data organisation

Limitations:

  • metadata is typed by hand, with no machine readable import
  • access is set per dataset, so a study with mixed access levels needs several datasets
  • the version history does not record who made an edit

Recommendations

  1. For open qualitative data: the GitHub to Zenodo workflow provides more flexibility, version control, and integration options. It suits researchers who are comfortable with technical tools and work with non-sensitive data. This package is an example.
  2. For sensitive or restricted data: SWISSUbase offers the necessary access controls. It serves researchers working with participant data that requires ethical oversight or graduated access.
  3. For mixed datasets: consider a hybrid approach, where documentation and non-sensitive materials use the GitHub workflow while sensitive data stays in SWISSUbase, linked through persistent identifiers.

Conclusion

Both workflows serve important roles in sharing qualitative data. The choice between them depends on data sensitivity, technical capacity, and institutional requirements. As Cloutier and Ravasi (2021) emphasise, transparency in data management enhances trustworthiness in qualitative research, and both platforms can achieve this in different ways.

References

Cloutier, Charlotte, and Davide Ravasi. 2021. “Using Tables to Enhance Trustworthiness in Qualitative Research.” Strategic Organization 19 (1): 113–33. https://doi.org/10.1177/1476127020979329.
Enriquez, Diana. 2024. “Publishing Publicly Available Interview Data: An Empirical Example of the Experience of Publishing Interview Data.” Frontiers in Sociology 9 (June). https://doi.org/10.3389/fsoc.2024.1157514.
